item.title: Tokyo spent 35 days "drowning" in rain and NASA satellites watched every drop fall over Japan
item.summary: For 35 days straight, Tokyo woke up to rain. From the final days of August through the last week of September 2026, the sky over central Japan ...
item.page_text:
For 35 days straight, Tokyo woke up to rain. From the final days of August through the last week of September 2026, the sky over central Japan simply refused to clear — a gray, unbroken stretch that turned the season’s rhythm on its head.
NASA satellites tracked it all in real time, capturing bands of rain sweeping across the region hour after hour. What they recorded raises a question worth asking: how does a city end up drowning for more than a month?
Tokyo’s previous record for consecutive rainy days stood at 33 — set in June and July of 2019, when the city endured an unusually persistent wet stretch through early summer . That mark held for seven years. Then, between August 27 and September 28, 2026, the streak climbed to 35 days and rewrote the books.
Breaking a rainfall continuity record in a megalopolis like Tokyo carries real weight. The city is home to roughly 14 million people within its core boundaries, and its infrastructure — drainage systems, transit networks, daily routines — is calibrated around seasonal norms. When those norms shatter, disruption compounds fast.
Worth noting: not every day in the streak was a downpour. Some registered only trace amounts of rain. But under meteorological standards, even minimal precipitation counts — and the continuity never broke. That uninterrupted thread is exactly what made 2026’s stretch historic.
The numbers stand on their own. Over those 35 days, Tokyo accumulated 629 millimeters — roughly 25 inches — of rainfall . That’s approximately three times the normal precipitation for that stretch of the season.
In little more than a month, the city received what it would typically expect across an entire season. The single most intense day came on September 21, when 156 millimeters (6 inches) fell within 24 hours — a volume that would be noteworthy on its own, let alone embedded inside a five-week rain event.
Seasonal averages reflect decades of accumulated climate data. They shape how cities plan for water management, agriculture, and public safety. When a single event triples that baseline, it exposes the limits of planning built around what used to be normal.
Sustained rainfall over 35 days doesn’t mean uniform rainfall. Within the streak, two typhoons — Krovanh and Dujuan — drove the most extreme precipitation episodes , and the peak on September 21 coincided with the passage of one of these systems.
Typhoons approaching or making landfall near Japan can dramatically intensify ongoing rainfall events. Their spiral bands push enormous volumes of moisture inland, often interacting with existing weather patterns to produce concentrated, heavy precipitation over short periods. Here, they transformed an already unusual wet stretch into something far more extreme.
Many days saw moderate or minimal rain — enough to keep the record alive, but not enough to cause major disruption on their own. The typhoon-driven episodes were the outliers that pushed totals into record territory.
While Tokyo residents tracked the rain from street level, NASA’s instruments were watching from orbit. The key tool was IMERG — the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement — which measures rainfall rates in millimeters per hour across wide geographic areas, providing a continuous, quantified picture of storm bands moving over central Japan.
Layered on top were true-color images from the VIIRS instrument aboard the NOAA-20 platform . VIIRS captures visible-light imagery, giving scientists and the public a recognizable, photographic-style view of cloud systems and storm structure.
Combining precipitation rate data with optical imagery creates something more useful than either dataset alone. You can see where rain is falling and how intensely — in near real time. NASA’s Worldview platform makes this kind of monitoring accessible, offering both current imagery and historical archives for tracking events like this one.
Records are data points. But they also ask questions. When a city like Tokyo — with sophisticated infrastructure and well-documented climate history — sees its rainfall continuity record broken by two full days, it’s worth pausing on what that signals.
Events of prolonged, extreme precipitation may not remain statistical outliers for long. As climate patterns shift, the boundary between “unusual” and “expected” tends to move — sometimes faster than planners anticipate. Satellite monitoring systems like IMERG and Worldview become more valuable precisely because they can track that movement, helping cities anticipate risks rather than simply react after the fact.
Whether a 35-day streak becomes a new benchmark or an early warning is a question Tokyo, and cities like it, may have to answer sooner than expected .

item.title: NASA Is About to Investigate What Lies Beneath a Giant Hole on the Moon - SciTechDaily
item.summary: NASA is backing a search for a hidden lunar cave that could reveal how ancient volcanic activity shaped the Moon.
item.page_text:
NASA is backing a search for a hidden lunar cave that could reveal how ancient volcanic activity shaped the Moon.
Scientists have gathered compelling evidence from lunar orbit for caves and lava tubes beneath the Moon’s surface, places that could one day shelter astronauts from radiation and extreme temperature swings.
NASA has selected a Planetary Science Institute (PSI)-led project to investigate whether a potentially large cave extends beyond the opening of the Marius Hill Pit (MHP).
A lander and rover will carry the instruments for the Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation, or GIMLI. Ground-penetrating radar will probe buried structures with radio waves, while seismic sensors will record how deliberately generated vibrations travel through the ground. The team will combine those readings with gravity measurements from a gravimeter and camera images of the surface and pit walls to investigate the surrounding material and estimate the size of any void it finds.
“It’s long been a desire of mine to reintroduce intentional active-source seismic methods to planetary science, as it has essentially not been done since the Apollo astronauts conducted the first seismic surveys on the Moon,” said GIMLI leader Than Putzig, PSI Associate Director and Senior Scientist. “Combining that method with ground-penetrating radar and gravity measurements makes it all the more exciting, as these methods together will allow us to get a much better understanding of subsurface properties — including the anticipated detection of a lava tube extending away from the Marius Hills pit.”
Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, will build much of the equipment, including instrumentation for the active-source seismic system, gravimeter, and cameras. As PSI’s commercial partner, the company will also provide project management services, integrate all the instruments onto the lander and rover, and jointly lead their lunar surface operations with PSI.
The Norwegian Space Agency will supply the ground-penetrating radar and partner with PSI on its work. Co-investigators from Boise State University, Johns Hopkins University, the Lunar and Planetary Institute, and the University of Oslo will also contribute to the project.
NASA will fund GIMLI through its Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) program, which sends scientific instruments to the Moon aboard spacecraft supplied by Commercial Lunar Payloads Services (CLPS) initiative providers. A CLPS provider will supply the lander and rover.
“GIMLI represents the type of ambitious planetary science that PSI was built to pursue,” said PSI Director and CEO Amanda Hendrix. “Than and his team are taking a scientific question we’ve been studying from orbit and have developed a way to investigate it directly on the Moon. We’re excited to have PSI leading this effort and to be partnering with NASA and Honeybee Robotics to learn more about the Moon and its volcanic past.”
MHP is a large hole in one of the Moon’s most volcanically diverse regions, and its walls expose layers of lava flows and regolith, the loose material covering the surface, that usually lie hidden underground. Studying these layers could reveal how lava traveled through the region during its long volcanic history and whether lengthy intervals separated eruptions. If GIMLI finds a cave or lava tube, its interior could preserve further evidence of the ancient volcanic activity that may have formed it.
“Confirming a substantial lava tube would give us an insight into how volcanism operated on the Moon,” explained Gareth Morgan, PSI Senior Scientist and Deputy Principal Investigator on the GIMLI program. “Lava tubes are a common feature of basaltic volcanism on Earth, so identifying them on the Moon means we could use knowledge of such terrestrial caves to better understand lunar history.”
Even if GIMLI finds no cave or lava tube, its measurements of the surrounding subsurface could help explain how the pit formed and clarify the geology and volcanic history of the site.
The project will be funded through NASA’s Payloads and Research Investigations on the Surface of the Moon (PRISM) program, which sends scientific instruments to the Moon on spacecraft provided by the Commercial Lunar Payloads Services (CLPS) initiative providers.

item.title: Mapped: The Male-to-Female Ratio in Every Country
item.summary: Explore gender ratios worldwide and why women outnumber men in Eastern Europe while Gulf countries have far more men.
item.page_text:
Women generally live longer than men, but that doesn’t mean every country has more women than men. In some countries, men outnumber women by more than two to one.
This visualization by Iswardi Ishak , using 2025 data from the United Nations Population Division Data Portal , maps the number of males per 100 females worldwide. A ratio above 100 indicates more males, while a figure below 100 indicates more females.
The following table shows the male-to-female population ratios of 237 countries and territories.
The figures reveal striking regional contrasts, from female-majority populations across much of Europe and Latin America to male-skewed populations in parts of Asia and the Middle East.
The scale of these differences is striking. Qatar has 245.9 males per 100 females, followed by the UAE (176.0) and Oman (166.0).
At the other extreme, Hong Kong has just 81.8 males per 100 females, followed by Guadeloupe (82.4) and Martinique (82.9).
Across Eastern Europe and former Soviet countries, women’s longer life expectancy is amplified by elevated male mortality. Cardiovascular disease, alcohol-related deaths, and historical demographic shocks have all contributed to the imbalance.
Pew Research Center also highlights the lasting demographic consequences of World War II and differences in male and female survival rates.
The imbalance is particularly pronounced among older age groups, where women substantially outnumber men. In countries such as Latvia, Lithuania, and Russia, decades of lower male life expectancy have contributed to some of the world’s most female-skewed populations.
The Persian Gulf presents the opposite pattern. Qatar, the UAE, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia have exceptionally male-heavy populations because they attract large numbers of predominantly male migrant workers, particularly in construction and infrastructure.
Many of these workers arrive from South Asian countries such as India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Nepal, often without their families. This creates an unusually large population of working-age men, pushing national gender ratios far beyond what natural birth patterns would produce.
Elsewhere in Asia, male-skewed populations in countries such as India and China reflect different forces, including historical son preference and sex-selective births. Unlike the Gulf states, these imbalances are driven more by long-term demographic and cultural factors than labor migration.
To explore another dimension of gender inequality, see Mapped: America’s Gender Earnings Gap by State , which examines differences in earnings between men and women across the United States.
This article was published as a part of Visual Capitalist's Creator Program , which features data-driven visuals from some of our favorite Creators around the world.

Explore the countries with the most Nobel Prizes, famous past winners, and the achievements recognized by the 2026 awards.
From groundbreaking scientific discoveries to achievements in literature and peace, the Nobel Prizes have recognized some of history’s most influential figures since 1901.
More than a century later, the ranking reveals which countries have accumulated the most awards, highlighting the global reach of the Nobel Prizes and the achievements behind them.
The data comes from Wikipedia and Nobel Prize records , as of October 2026. Some laureates are associated with more than one country, so national totals can overlap.
The United States has nearly three times as many Nobel Prizes as the UK, which ranks second. Beyond the four leading countries, the ranking becomes considerably tighter, with Sweden and Japan sharing fifth place at 34 each.
American Nobel laureates span a wide range of disciplines and historical periods. President Theodore Roosevelt received the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize for helping negotiate an end to the Russo-Japanese War, while Martin Luther King Jr. was honored in 1964 for his nonviolent struggle against racial discrimination.
In literature, Ernest Hemingway won in 1954 for his influential storytelling, including The Old Man and the Sea . More recently, Barack Obama received the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts to strengthen international diplomacy, while Bob Dylan won the 2016 Literature Prize for his contributions to American songwriting.
Polish-born Marie Curie, who built her scientific career in France, shared the 1903 Physics Prize for research on radioactivity and won the 1911 Chemistry Prize for her work on radium and polonium.
Albert Einstein received the 1921 Physics Prize for his contributions to theoretical physics, especially his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect, rather than his theory of relativity.
Scotland’s Alexander Fleming shared the 1945 Medicine Prize with Ernst Boris Chain and Howard Florey for the discovery of penicillin and its effectiveness against infectious diseases.
In South Africa, Nelson Mandela and F.W. de Klerk shared the 1993 Peace Prize for helping bring about a peaceful end to apartheid and laying the foundations for democratic government.
Kenyan environmentalist Wangari Maathai made history in 2004 when she became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. She was recognized for her contributions to sustainable development, democracy, and peace.
Her Green Belt Movement mobilized women to plant trees, helping plant more than 30 million while connecting environmental protection with women’s rights and stronger communities.
